Fixes #27323
#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR resolves issue #27323 by ensuring that rewrite(abs) correctly maps to rewrite(Abs) for consistency when using the built-in abs function. @asmeurer @oscarbenjamin 

#### Other comments
Changes Made:

- Updated the rewrite method to handle abs as a special case, redirecting it to Abs.
- Added a test case in sympy/core/tests/test_basic.py to confirm that rewrite(abs) produces the same output as rewrite(Abs).

  * Corrected a semantical error in the conversion between volt and statvolt which
    reported the volt as being larger than the statvolt.

Fixes #27323
#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR resolves issue #27323 by ensuring that rewrite(abs) correctly maps to rewrite(Abs) for consistency when using the built-in abs function. @asmeurer @oscarbenjamin 

#### Other comments
Changes Made:

- Updated the rewrite method to handle abs as a special case, redirecting it to Abs.
- Added a test case in sympy/core/tests/test_basic.py to confirm that rewrite(abs) produces the same output as rewrite(Abs).

Fixes #27323
#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR resolves issue #27323 by ensuring that rewrite(abs) correctly maps to rewrite(Abs) for consistency when using the built-in abs function. @asmeurer @oscarbenjamin 

#### Other comments
Changes Made:

- Updated the rewrite method to handle abs as a special case, redirecting it to Abs.
- Added a test case in sympy/core/tests/test_basic.py to confirm that rewrite(abs) produces the same output as rewrite(Abs).

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR resolves issue #27323 by ensuring that rewrite(abs) correctly maps to rewrite(Abs) for consistency when using the built-in abs function. @asmeurer @oscarbenjamin 

#### Other comments
Changes Made:

- Updated the rewrite method to handle abs as a special case, redirecting it to Abs.
- Added a test case in sympy/core/tests/test_basic.py to confirm that rewrite(abs) produces the same output as rewrite(Abs).

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR resolves issue #27323 by ensuring that rewrite(abs) correctly maps to rewrite(Abs) for consistency when using the built-in abs function. @asmeurer @oscarbenjamin 

#### Other comments
Changes Made:

- Updated the rewrite method to handle abs as a special case, redirecting it to Abs.
- Added a test case in sympy/core/tests/test_basic.py to confirm that rewrite(abs) produces the same output as rewrite(Abs).

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR resolves issue #27323 by ensuring that rewrite(abs) correctly maps to rewrite(Abs) for consistency when using the built-in abs function. @asmeurer @oscarbenjamin 

#### Other comments
Changes Made:

- Updated the rewrite method to handle abs as a special case, redirecting it to Abs.
- Added a test case in sympy/core/tests/test_basic.py to confirm that rewrite(abs) produces the same output as rewrite(Abs).

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR resolves issue #27323 by ensuring that rewrite(abs) correctly maps to rewrite(Abs) for consistency when using the built-in abs function. @asmeurer @oscarbenjamin 

#### Other comments
Changes Made:

- Updated the rewrite method to handle abs as a special case, redirecting it to Abs.
- Added a test case in sympy/core/tests/test_basic.py to confirm that rewrite(abs) produces the same output as rewrite(Abs).

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR resolves issue #27323 by ensuring that rewrite(abs) correctly maps to rewrite(Abs) for consistency when using the built-in abs function. @asmeurer @oscarbenjamin 

#### Other comments
Changes Made:

- Updated the rewrite method to handle abs as a special case, redirecting it to Abs.
- Added a test case in sympy/core/tests/test_basic.py to confirm that rewrite(abs) produces the same output as rewrite(Abs).

This PR is based on conversations with @oscarbenjamin in https://github.com/pyodide/pyodide/pull/5098 and a subsequent discussion with @asmeurer a fortnight ago. The Pyodide test suite was last discussed in #24920 and https://github.com/sympy/sympy/pull/25394#issuecomment-1650410409. 

Furthermore, this PR can potentially close #24306.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed

This PR aims to re-enable the Pyodide CI job that runs the SymPy test suite inside a Pyodide runtime and fix some of the issues with reliability and flaky tests. I've removed `bin/test_pyodide.mjs` and the related code for it, and removed imports for `pyodide_js` across the codebase where necessary. The rest of the changes are just related to code cleanup and adding skip markers for a few tests. The Pyodide virtual environment that has been added should be more closer to a Pythonic test invocation and more useful if wanting to run the tests locally. While a GHA runner will be slower, I'm able to run the test suite minus the slow and "tooslow" tests without hiccups in thirty minutes when testing locally (side note: the "tooslow" tests take way too long in Pyodide, up to the order of eight minutes for a single test – they should definitely be disabled!). Additionally, the `@skip_under_pyodide` decorator added in #24892 has been simplified.

SymPy is a pure Python package and testing it under Pyodide may not have been useful, but since a CI job previously existed and if the test suite can run reliably here, both of those points make an additional case for including it back again :D 

P.S. It's always good to have a CI job in general (as long as it doesn't strain SymPy's existing infrastructure) because there are some "slow" tests that I noted were failing and have been previously noted to fail (which I haven't tried to fix here – I could try them in a separate PR after this since they might be tricky).

#### Other comments

The tests are split into a GitHub Actions matrix with four groups with `pytest-split`, as it was in the previous iteration of the test suite before it was disabled. There is a caching mechanism where the test durations are individually collected and stored in a GitHub Actions cache with a persistent key, so that it is always saved and restored every time the workflow is triggered. This seems to work quite well when a cache hits (which will be every time) when I was testing this in a PR on my fork (https://github.com/agriyakhetarpal/sympy/pull/1), but I can let go of this if needed and switch to the existing periodic update for the durations (the durations for Pyodide will be stored and saved separately, however).

Due to these additional jobs, I've added all this under a separate workflow in `emscripten.yml` and not in the standard `runtests.yml` file (but I'm happy to move things around if I'm requested to). 

With the caching here, all four test groups complete in ~19 minutes.

Fixes #27156


#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
This PR updates the residue function to utilize the modified nseries method for series expansion. The nseries method now captures series expansions in both positive and negative directions, allowing for accurate residue calculation. The residue is defined as the coefficient of 
1/(𝑥−𝑥0) in the power series expansion around 
𝑥=𝑥0.
#### Other comments
This change enhances the robustness of residue calculations, ensuring correct behavior in scenarios where series behavior differs in positive and negative directions.

#### Release Notes

series
Updated the residue function to utilize the modified nseries method for series expansion, allowing residue calculations from both positive and negative directions.
Improved handling of coefficients in series expansion to ensure accurate residue extraction.

Fixes #26513 
#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
sign function in gruntz gave erroneous results for negative logarithmic arguments. Refactored `set_signs` in limits to let pass expressions returning NotImplementedError for gruntz to operate directly on abs functions . Made this separate PR for this issue as suggested in  #26749.

Now if that's the case I think we can eliminate the cdir from these methods completely.
As I said above, what does the series method do ? 
1) It transformation the function and the cdir at hand and while making calls to `_eval_nseries` only passes cdir = 1
2) Once we get back the series, we just need to re-transform it back (which might be something like "cdir * output from 1")

This is not being done for other methods like `as_leading_term`, `leadterm`.
I sense if we change the other higher level methods, it will be much easier and help us remove lot of redundancy
1) We would just need the re-transform logic (this won't even be as much as for series cause we can calculate series at infinity and points other than `0` ... this won't be the case for leadterm .... should be very convinient)
2) The helpers only deal with `cdir=1`

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

  * Implemented besselk series expansion for non-integer order

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

  * Corrected a semantical error in the conversion between volt and statvolt which

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

Describe your issue.

More of a doubt than a bug

I was executing the following on a pyodide repl
```
>>> import scipy
from scipy.linalg import _fblas as fblas, get_blas_funcs, toeplitz, solve
>>> f = getattr(fblas, 'cdotu', None)
>>> print(f([3j, -4, 3-4j], [2, 3, 1]))
The cause of the fatal error was:
RuntimeError: null function or function signature mismatch
```

This shows a function signature mismatch. 
1) The function being called `call_indirect (param i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)`
2) How the function is defined `(func $f2pywrapcdotu_ (;227;) (export "f2pywrapcdotu_") (param $var0 i32) (param $var1 i32) (param $var2 i32) (param $var3 i32) (param $var4 i32) (param $var5 i32) (param $var6 i32) (param $var7 i32) (result i32)`

The first one passes `6` parameters and the second one requires `8`

This raises a confusion about the signatures & definitions for `dotu` and `dotu` wrappers

For eg
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/8048c1e93c6226a6ea3e2395560e6b23f81ff0f8/scipy/linalg/cython_blas_signatures.txt#L6-L7


Though Something that looks correct to me is the following
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/e83749437f2617b19e4d133c80a11183b1486fab/scipy/linalg/fblas_l1.pyf.src#L329

The difference between the two is basically the offsets for the arrays `x` and `y` basically `offx` and `offy`. I think this might be the answer for the 2 missing input parameters that causes the signature mismatch in my example above.

Not sure if I analyzed this correctly and would like some help here

Describe your issue.

More of a doubt than a bug

I was executing the following on a pyodide repl
```
>>> import scipy
from scipy.linalg import _fblas as fblas, get_blas_funcs, toeplitz, solve
>>> f = getattr(fblas, 'cdotu', None)
>>> print(f([3j, -4, 3-4j], [2, 3, 1]))
The cause of the fatal error was:
RuntimeError: null function or function signature mismatch
```

This shows a function signature mismatch. 
1) The function being called `call_indirect (param i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)`
2) How the function is defined `(func $f2pywrapcdotu_ (;227;) (export "f2pywrapcdotu_") (param $var0 i32) (param $var1 i32) (param $var2 i32) (param $var3 i32) (param $var4 i32) (param $var5 i32) (param $var6 i32) (param $var7 i32) (result i32)`

The first one passes `6` parameters and the second one requires `8`

This raises a confusion about the signatures & definitions for `dotu` and `dotu` wrappers

For eg
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/8048c1e93c6226a6ea3e2395560e6b23f81ff0f8/scipy/linalg/cython_blas_signatures.txt#L6-L7


Though Something that looks correct to me is the following
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/blob/e83749437f2617b19e4d133c80a11183b1486fab/scipy/linalg/fblas_l1.pyf.src#L329

The difference between the two is basically the offsets for the arrays `x` and `y` basically `offx` and `offy`. I think this might be the answer for the 2 missing input parameters that causes the signature mismatch in my example above.

Not sure if I analyzed this correctly and would like some help here


### SciPy/NumPy/Python version and system information

```shell
>>> print(scipy.__version__)
1.12.0
>>> print(np.__version__)
1.26.4
>>> print(sys.version_info)
sys.version_info(major=3, minor=12, micro=1, releaselevel='final', serial=0)
```

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
SymPy currently in many cases auto simplifes terms of the form exp(log(...)), this behaviour causes problems with workings of gruntz as this complicates the comparison of terms in their respective comparability classes. This branch solves this anomaly by ensuring that every symbolic pow term is expressed in  the form `exp(exp*log(base))`

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
SymPy currently in many cases auto simplifes terms of the form exp(log(...)), this behaviour causes problems with workings of gruntz as this complicates the comparison of terms in their respective comparability classes. This branch solves this anomaly by ensuring that every symbolic pow term is expressed in  the form `exp(exp*log(base))`

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

  * Fixed a bug with log of integers. Formerly, `log(-x)` incorrectly gave `-log(x)`.

* physics.units
  * Corrected a semantical error in the conversion between volt and statvolt which
    reported the volt as being larger than the statvolt.

or if no release note(s) should be included use:

NO ENTRY

See https://github.com/sympy/sympy/wiki/Writing-Release-Notes for more

* functions
  * Implemented besselk series expansion for non-integer order
  * besselk: fixed calculation of leading term for non-integer negative orders
<!-- END RELEASE NOTES -->

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
SymPy currently in many cases auto simplifes terms of the form exp(log(...)), this behaviour causes problems with workings of gruntz as this complicates the comparison of terms in their respective comparability classes. This branch solves this anomaly by ensuring that every symbolic pow term is expressed in  the form `exp(exp*log(base))`

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
SymPy currently in many cases auto simplifes terms of the form exp(log(...)), this behaviour causes problems with workings of gruntz as this complicates the comparison of terms in their respective comparability classes. This branch solves this anomaly by ensuring that every symbolic pow term is expressed in  the form `exp(exp*log(base))`

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
SymPy currently in many cases auto simplifes terms of the form exp(log(...)), this behaviour causes problems with workings of gruntz as this complicates the comparison of terms in their respective comparability classes. This branch solves this anomaly by ensuring that every symbolic pow term is expressed in  the form `exp(exp*log(base))`

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
SymPy currently in many cases auto simplifes terms of the form exp(log(...)), this behaviour causes problems with workings of gruntz as this complicates the comparison of terms in their respective comparability classes. This branch solves this anomaly by ensuring that every symbolic pow term is expressed in  the form `exp(exp*log(base))`

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
SymPy currently in many cases auto simplifes terms of the form exp(log(...)), this behaviour causes problems with workings of gruntz as this complicates the comparison of terms in their respective comparability classes. This branch solves this anomaly by ensuring that every symbolic pow term is expressed in  the form `exp(exp*log(base))`

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

Yes I get it. Wasn't my favourite thing to work on when I was looking into it couple of years ago. But answering your question, I think it is needed at some places. Mainly being this 
https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/72f210ce2e9c164fab5280b10df2f351a6e0dbf5/sympy/core/expr.py#L2996-L3015

So any use of the series function unless it is of the form `series(f(x), x, 0, dir = "+")` uses transformation that involves substituion (which would involve a substitution in the order term too)

But then I think not everything was clear as to how substituion works for the order class which led to issues and also use of solveset and/or limit. The solveset was used to handle the basic case of `Order(x**2).subs(x, y - 1)`

{"action":"opened","issue":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/sympy/sympy/issues/26957","repository_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/sympy/sympy","labels_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/sympy/sympy/issues/26957/labels{/name}","comments_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/sympy/sympy/issues/26957/comments","events_url":"https://api.github.com/repos/sympy/sympy/issues/26957/events","html_url":"https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/26957","id":2463274013,"node_id":"I_kwDOAAnGFs6S0pQd","number":26957,"title":"Introduce a Series class instead of using Add terms with Order","user":{"login":"anutosh491","id":87052487,"node_id":"MDQ6VXNlcjg3MDUyNDg3","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/87052487?v=4","gravatar_id":"","url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491","html_url":"https://github.com/anutosh491","followers_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/followers","following_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/following{/other_user}","gists_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/gists{/gist_id}","starred_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/starred{/owner}{/repo}","subscriptions_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/subscriptions","organizations_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/orgs","repos_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/repos","events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/events{/privacy}","received_events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/received_events","type":"User","site_admin":false},"labels":[],"state":"open","locked":false,"assignee":null,"assignees":[],"milestone":null,"comments":0,"created_at":"2024-08-13T12:47:46Z","updated_at":"2024-08-13T12:47:46Z","closed_at":null,"author_association":"MEMBER","active_lock_reason":null,"body":"              > This is a reason I am sometimes confused if the series should even be addition of functions + an order term to make an object of the add class (rather than having its own class).

There is no need to be confused about this. Implementing series as an Add with an O term is a bad idea.

A Series should be a special object of its own and it should be like Poly rather than like Expr. The internal representation should be like a Poly i.e. with an actual ordered list of coefficients. The coefficients should be represented using domain elements in a canonical form, always expanded etc just like for Poly. There should be no need to waste time debating whether to call expand, cancel etc because the domain elements are always canonical.

The ring_series module shows how to do this but is too low-level (gh-26100). It needs to be wrapped in something higher-level like Poly. Also python-flint should be used when possible:
```python
In [7]: from flint import fmpq_series

In [8]: x = fmpq_series([0, 1])

In [9]: x
Out[9]: x + O(x^10)

In [10]: 1/(x + 1)
Out[10]: 1 + (-1)*x + x^2 + (-1)*x^3 + x^4 + (-1)*x^5 + x^6 + (-1)*x^7 + x^8 + (-1)*x^9 + O(x^10)

In [11]: x.exp()
Out[11]: 1 + x + 1/2*x^2 + 1/6*x^3 + 1/24*x^4 + 1/120*x^5 + 1/720*x^6 + 1/5040*x^7 + 1/40320*x^8 + 1/362880*x^9 + O(x^10)
```
It is much faster:
```python
In [1]: from flint import ctx

In [2]: ctx.cap = 1000

In [3]: from flint import fmpq_series

In [4]: x = fmpq_series([0, 1])

In [5]: %time r = x.exp()
CPU times: user 5.04 ms, sys: 79 μs, total: 5.12 ms
Wall time: 6.18 ms

In [6]: len(r)
Out[6]: 1000
```
Compare:
```python
In [12]: %time ok = exp(x).series(x, n=1000)
CPU times: user 19.2 s, sys: 23.3 ms, total: 19.3 s
Wall time: 19.3 s
```
That's 3000x slower.

It should be possible to have multivariate series as well (gh-25483).

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
SymPy currently in many cases auto simplifes terms of the form exp(log(...)), this behaviour causes problems with workings of gruntz as this complicates the comparison of terms in their respective comparability classes. This branch solves this anomaly by ensuring that every symbolic pow term is expressed in  the form `exp(exp*log(base))`

I came across an issue which is similar to the one above , I searched whether any similar/related issue has been reported already and found one on the google groups . `gruntz` is responsible for this .Not too sure about the fix though !
```
>>> x = Symbol('x', real=True, positive=True)
>>> m = Symbol('m', real=True, positive=True)
>>> limit((log(E + 1/x) - 1)**(1 - sqrt(E + 1/x)), x, oo)
0
>>> gruntz((log(E + 1/x) - 1)**(1 - sqrt(E + 1/x)), x, oo)
0
```
Close relatives of the expression work fine 
```
>>> limit((log(E + 1/x) )**(1 - sqrt(E + 1/x)), x, oo)
1
>>> limit((log(E + 1/x) - 1)**(- sqrt(E + 1/x)), x, oo)
oo
```
Pic from wolfram for reference
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/87052487/151969221-3d80ddcf-d911-4712-a02c-eb7743e224d5.png)

As this has already been reported on the google group , it might have been raised before . Though I did a basic check for myself, if found to be reported earlier ...feel free to close . Thanks!

Fixes #26523
Fixes #26707


#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed

Added regression tests
Implemented the functions _eval_is_finite and _eval_as_leading_term for the lerchphi class.
`lerchphi._eval_is_finite` has been implemented with finite complex numbers in mind. A possible extension to handle infinite arguments is left for the future.
The divergences considered are the following:
$$\Phi(0, s, a) = \frac{1}{a^s}$$
Which diverges when $a=0$ and $s \in \mathbb{R}^+$.
When $z \neq 0$, the function diverges when $a \in - \mathbb{N}$ and $s \in \mathbb{R}^+$.
$$\Phi(z, s, -k) = \sum\_{n=0}^\infty \frac{z^n}{(n-k)^s}$$
Finally, for $z=1$, the function has the same poles as the zeta function: $s = 1$.
No analytic continuation has been considered, except for $\Phi(1,s,a)=\zeta(s,a)$.
`lerchphi._eval_as_leading_term` has been implemented. It handles the following limits:
$$\lim\_{z \to 1} \Phi(z, 1, a_0) = -\log(\log(z)) - \gamma_E - \psi(a_0)$$
If $s \in \mathbb{N}^+$ or $\Re(s_0) > 1$:
$$\lim\_{(z, s, a) \to (1, s_0, a_0)} \Phi(z, s, a) = \zeta(s_0, a_0)$$
If $\Re(s_0) < 1$:
$$\lim\_{(z, s) \to (1, s_0)} \Phi(z, s, a) = \Gamma(1-s) (-\log(z))^{s-1}$$
If $a_0 \in -\mathbb{N}$ and $s \in \mathbb{R}^+$:
$$\lim\_{a \to a_0} \Phi(z, s, a) = \frac{z^{-a_0}}{(a-a_0)^s}$$

Added new functionality to the `zeta._eval_as_leading_term` method.
It adds the following cases:
$$\lim\_{(s,a) \to (s_0, a_0)} \zeta(s, a) = \zeta(s_0, a_0), \qquad \text{if} \qquad s_0 \neq 1$$
$$\lim\_{(s,a) \to (1, a_0)} \zeta(s, a) = \frac{1}{s-1}$$
Added tests for all the new changes.

#### Other comments

Road map:

Following the discussion at https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/26523, in order to solve the bug with the integral
$$\int\_0^1 \frac{1-t^z}{1-t} \mathrm{d}t = \psi(z+1) + \gamma_E$$
We need to correctly compute the following limit:
$$\lim\_{t \to 1^-} \left\[-t^{z+1}\Phi(t, 1, z+1) - \log(t - 1)\right\] = \psi(z+1) + \gamma_E - i \pi$$
Sympy currently gives the wrong result for this limit, which causes the bug. To avoid returning the wrong value, we need the following:
We first need sympy to identify that $\Phi(1, 1, z+1)$ is infinite to avoid simply substituting $t=1$. This requires the implementation of `lerchphi._eval_is_finite`.
This is enough to solve the bug in the `gruntz` algorithm. However, Sympy will also try to solve the limit using the `heuristics` algorithm, which also has this bug.
The `heuristics` algorithm seems to just do the substitution $t = 1$. So a check to make sure the result is finite is needed.
With these, the integral should no longer return the wrong result but rather either raise an error or return the unevaluated result.

In order to compute the correct limit, an implementation of `lerchphi._eval_as_leading_term` is needed, which should be able to correctly identify
$$\lim\_{\varepsilon \to 0^+} \Phi(1-\varepsilon, 1, z+1) = -\log(\varepsilon) - \gamma_E - \psi(z+1)$$
Finally, a simplification needs to be added somewhere to simplify
```python
(-t*t**z*z*lerchphi(t, 1, z + 1)*gamma(z + 1)/gamma(z + 2)
 - t*t**z*lerchphi(t, 1, z + 1)*gamma(z + 1)/gamma(z + 2)
 - log(t - 1))
```
to
```python
-t**(z + 1)*lerchphi(t, 1, z + 1) - log(t - 1)
```

I guess that's not required. Something like the above can return `I`

What I think should happen for functions like `sign` or `arg` etc is the following. So we can see that there is no real difference in what the series and the leading term should return for these functions.
So what we can do here is shift the code from `_eval_nseries` (which I did go through and think should work) to `_eval_as_leading_term` something like this 
```

    def _eval_as_leading_term(self, x, logx=None, cdir=0):
        arg0 = self.args[0]
        x0 = arg0.subs(x, 0)
        if x0 != 0:
            return self.func(x0)
        if cdir != 0:
            cdir = arg0.dir(x, cdir)
        return -S.One if re(cdir) < 0 else S.One     
```
and then we just use that in the _eval_nseries call, maybe something like this (you might need to verify !!!)
```
    def _eval_nseries(self, x, n, logx):
        c, _ = self.args[0].as_leading_term(x).as_coeff_exponent(x)
        return self.func(c.limit(x, 0))     
```
I think someone as simple as this would also do the job
```
    def _eval_nseries(self, x, n, logx, cdir=0):
        return self._eval_as_leading_term(x, logx=logx, cdir=cdir)
```

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Series expansion for besselk (usually denoted as $K_\nu$) about the origin.
(<https://functions.wolfram.com/Bessel-TypeFunctions/BesselK/06/01/04/01/01/0003/>). Earlier, it was implemented only for integer orders.

This PR also fixes `besselk._eval_as_leading_term` for negative non-integer orders.

#### Other comments
I have also fixed a bug in the series expansion for integer orders (it was sometimes returning the wrong `Order` object), and added tests.

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
On Master
```
>>> x = Symbol('x')
... f = Function('f')
... print limit(f(x), x, 4)  
f(4)

>>> func = x*y*y / (x*x + y**4)
... func2 = func.subs(y, f(x)) 
... limit(func2, x, 0) # won't work generally eg f(x) = sqrt(x)
0
```
Obviously these results are not what one would expect as we don't make any assumptions about the function and its continuity, hence there should be heuristics for the same !

On Committed branch
```
>>> x = Symbol('x')
>>> f = Function('f')
>>> limit(f(x), x, 4)
Traceback (most recent call last):
NotImplementedError: Result depends on the continuity of f(x) at point 4
>>> 
>>> y = Symbol('y')
>>> func = x*y*y / (x*x + y**4)
>>> func2 = func.subs(y, f(x))
>>>
>>> limit(func2, x, 0)
Traceback (most recent call last):
NotImplementedError: Result depends on the continuity of x*f(x)**2/(x**2 + f(x)**4) at point 0
>>>
>>> func3 = func.subs(y, sqrt(x))
>>> limit(func3, x, 0)
1/2
```

{"action":"created","comment":{"url":"https://api.github.com/repos/sympy/sympy/pulls/comments/1730269412","pull_request_review_id":2259177293,"id":1730269412,"node_id":"PRRC_kwDOAAnGFs5nIdDk","diff_hunk":"@@ -257,11 +257,11 @@ def doit(self, **hints): if e.is_Order: return Order(limit(e.expr, z, z0), *e.args[1:]) - cdir = 0 + cdir = S.Zero if str(dir) == "+": - cdir = 1 + cdir = S.One elif str(dir) == "-": - cdir = -1 + cdir = S.NegativeOne ","path":"sympy/series/limits.py","commit_id":"b6bb7ae6cd51ee8c45671a2a3064925ea9e10d7c","original_commit_id":"b6bb7ae6cd51ee8c45671a2a3064925ea9e10d7c","user":{"login":"anutosh491","id":87052487,"node_id":"MDQ6VXNlcjg3MDUyNDg3","avatar_url":"https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/87052487?v=4","gravatar_id":"","url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491","html_url":"https://github.com/anutosh491","followers_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/followers","following_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/following{/other_user}","gists_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/gists{/gist_id}","starred_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/starred{/owner}{/repo}","subscriptions_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/subscriptions","organizations_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/orgs","repos_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/repos","events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/events{/privacy}","received_events_url":"https://api.github.com/users/anutosh491/received_events","type":"User","site_admin":false},"body":"Okay Answering the above doubts/questions raised (@oscarbenjamin, @arnabnandikgp) 1) What is `cdir` ? As Arnab explains above (I think even I would have explained in a similar way) cdir stands for "complex direction" 2) Does that mean `cdir` or rather the "direction of approach" can be complex ? Absolutely (as arnab said this would mostly come into picture for functions having branch cuts) ``` >>> asin(x + 2)._eval_nseries(x, 4, None, I) -asin(2) + pi + sqrt(3)*I*x/3 - sqrt(3)*I*x**2/9 + sqrt(3)*I*x**3/18 + O(x**4) >>> asin(x + 2)._eval_as_leading_term(x, None, I) pi - asin(2) ``` These are results that were heavily tested by Kalevi and myself during my GSoC (https://github.com/sympy/sympy/pull/23715) As I shall explain below there is also a way to justify why `asin(I*x + 2)._eval_as_leading_term(x, None, 1)` should equal to `asin(x + 2)._eval_as_leading_term(x, None, I)` 3) Numerically what values of cdir can affect a series/leadterm computation ? As far as I know only 4 values (**1, -1, I, -I**) can affect a computation. Series and Leading term implementation for functions where cdir actually plays a role were mostly written by me and @sachin-4099 (during his gsoc in 2020) and mostly whenever we need to decide on cdir i) We first check if it's real or imaginary ii) Then we check if the positive or negative (or imaginary part of cdir postive or negative if cdir is imaginary) So technically no scalar multiplication or a shift for eg `cdir = 2`, `cdir = 2* I` or `cdir = I + 1` matters 4) So how does `cdir = 0` contribute ? Technically it doesn't and just acts as a placeholder, cause sympy didn't give great results for series or limits for functions where actually the direction of approach matters before 2022. This can be shown by taking simple cases like logarithms or inverse trigs having branch cuts/points. Some tests I wrote in 2022 ``` assert log(-2*x).as_leading_term(x, cdir=1, logx=p) == p + log(2) + I*pi assert log(-2*x).as_leading_term(x, cdir=-1, logx=p) == p + log(2) - I*pi assert asin(1/x).as_leading_term(x, cdir=1) == I*log(x) + pi/2 - I*log(2) assert asin(1/x).as_leading_term(x, cdir=-1) == -I*log(x) - 3*pi/2 + I*log(2) ``` So I think when _eval_as_leading_term or _eval_nseries was framed, there was a vision that a parameter encapsulating "the direction of appraoch" would play a role in the future but during that time nothing was addressed hence I think a default value of `cdir = 0` was used. Hence according to my discussions with Kalevi (all these are well documentation on the gitter channel as we had all the discussions there) ... I can claim that `cdir = 0` implies nothing but `cdir = 1` or rather we consider "a real right hand direction of appraoch towards origin" by default just like we use dir = "+" by default for Limits. 5) When did the shift from `cdir = 0` to `cdir = 1` happen ? This started from the algorithm Kalevi and I framed for calculating leading term and series for simple functions like pow, sqrt, log etc that had branch cuts. These formed the fundamental building blocks for other functions have branch cuts like inverse trig, inverse hyperbolic etc. The algorithm can be read here (https://github.com/sympy/sympy/pull/23592#issue-1262779264). Pasting an image too 6) Lastly as I said above, we can justify as to why `asin(I*x + 2)._eval_as_leading_term(x, None, 1)` should equal to `asin(x + 2)._eval_as_leading_term(x, None, I)` This is because as the algorithm says we first do `x = cdir*t` where where `t` is `real` and `positive` and the idea I think it to transform every direction to a "real right hand side of approach" and then do the computation. This helps us with `dir` too as it can only be "+" or "-" . So although we don't have a complex dir like a complex cdir, we can still do ``` >>> limit(asin(I*x + 2), x, 0, "+") pi - asin(2) ``` and think of this being the leading term for asin(x + 2) but with a complex direction of approach. Not sure everything I wrote above makes sense as I had worked on it a couple years back but this should be all I know. > cdir=0 and so we need to be clear about what this means. It is either analogous to +-

Nope, `cdir = 0` does not stand for `dir = "+"`. I had the same doubt during my GSoC but my mentors Kalevi and Sidharth made that clear during proposal review (hence this is documented in my proposal too)

> I think that there is some value in being able to specify explicitly "any complex direction" rather than getting a series that is only for a single direction like +. 

1) You can explicitly specify the direction of interest for series (series supports both `dir` and `cdir`). So you can have 
```
>>> asin(x + 2).series(x, n = 3, cdir = I)
-asin(2) + pi + sqrt(3)*I*x/3 - sqrt(3)*I*x**2/9 + O(x**3)
>>> asin(x + 2).series(x, n = 3, cdir = 1)
-I*log(sqrt(3) + 2) + pi/2 - I*x*(3 + 2*sqrt(3))/(3*sqrt(3) + 6) - I*x**2*(-7*sqrt(3) - 12)/(36*sqrt(3) + 63) + O(x**3)
```

All these results were verified during my GSoC so I am confident of how cdir works here.

2) I don't think we can do something like `sin(x).series(x, dir = "+", cdir = -1)`
We might not return an error if that's done but we assume the user would know that this doesn't make sense.

3) I think cdir is given more power/weightage as it is can take up more values.
`dir` can be `+`, `-` but `cdir` can be `1`, `-1`, `I`, `-I`. Hence we have 

https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/e676df8ded885babe62bd31bec5db8c96b7480e7/sympy/core/expr.py#L2979-L2992

So basically 
if cdir is defined, then frame dir based on cdir 
and if cdir is 0, then frame cdir based on dir.

> It may be that the best default behaviour though is to treat cdir = 1 if that is already implicitly assumed in places...

Yuss, most computations are done that way. For example series at `oo` will have a `dir = "-"` direction of approach but we transform this to series at `0` with `dir = "+"` and `cdir = 1`
https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/e676df8ded885babe62bd31bec5db8c96b7480e7/sympy/core/expr.py#L2996-L2999

So I can say that most calls internally take care of the transformation (substitution for `x` by `1/x` or whatever) followed by a transformation for `cdir = 1` (even for the imaginary cdir case). I think atleast for starters we should stick to this.

1) > The places that have zero in the code should probably use something like None to more clearly show that it just a default representing no value provided.

This doesn't make sense to me fully. Cause at the highest level if we aim for using None for cdir, we end up with this for series

Fixes #21029

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed
Currently on Master

```
from sympy import *
x = Symbol('x')
z = Symbol('z')
>>> limit((exp(x)-1)/x, x, z) # Not the correct output 
(exp(z) - 1)/z
>>> limit((exp(x)-1)/x, x, z).subs(z, 0)
nan
>>> limit(ln(1+x)/x, x, z)
log(z + 1)/z
>>> limit(ln(1+x)/x, x, z).subs(z, 0) 
nan
>>> limit(sin(x)/x, x, z)
sin(z)/z
>>> limit(sin(x)/x, x, z).subs(z, 0)
nan
```
Hence whenever the point is passed as Symbol , we get wrong answers for the same . This is because the returned answers need a piecewise output and something like `sin(z)/z` is not the correct output for  `limit(sin(x)/x, x, z)`. This had to be addressed through a piecewise implementation as discussed in the issue .
The issue reported is basically the same thing 
```
In [79]: limit(cc/x,x,z)                                                                                                                           
Out[79]: 
 z    
ℯ  - 1
──────
 4⋅z  

In [80]: limit(cc/x,x,z).subs(z,0)                                                                                                                 
Out[80]: nan
```

So as I couldn't find any explicit check for `z0.is_Symbol` in `limits.py`, I realized something like this hasn't been implemented yet. Hence I've added a function `return_peicewise` and I've added a check at whichever places we could get an expression like above as output ! The implemented function would return a Piecewise Limit Function with a limit check at all concerned points starting from `-oo` to `oo`
Some examples being

```
>>> limit(sin(x)/x, x, z)
Piecewise((1, Eq(z, 0)), (sin(z)/z, True))
>>> limit(sin(x)/x, x, z).subs(z, 0)
1

>>> limit( sin(x)/(x**2 -4) , x, z)
Piecewise((oo, Eq(z, -2) | Eq(z, 2)), (sin(z)/((z - 2)*(z + 2)), True))

>>> limit((1- cos(x))/x**2, x, z)
Piecewise((1/2, Eq(z, 0)), (-(cos(z) - 1)/z**2, True))

>>> limit(1/(5 - x)**3, x, z, dir="+")
Piecewise((-oo, Eq(z, 5)), ((5 - z)**(-3), True))

>>> limit(1/(5 - x)**3, x, z, dir="-")
Piecewise((oo, Eq(z, 5)), ((5 - z)**(-3), True))

>>> limit(log(1 + x)/x, x, z)
Piecewise((0, Eq(z, -oo)), (oo, Eq(z, -1)), (1, Eq(z, 0)), (0, Eq(z, oo)), (log(z + 1)/z, True))

>>> limit((1 + x)/x, x, z)
Piecewise((1, Eq(z, -oo)), (oo, Eq(z, 0)), (1, Eq(z, oo)), ((z + 1)/z, True))

>>> limit((1 + 1/x)**x, x, z)
Piecewise((E, Eq(z, -oo)), (1, Eq(z, 0)), (E, Eq(z, oo)), ((1 + 1/z)**z, True))

>>> limit((1 + 1/(x**2 -4))**x, x, z)
Piecewise((1, Eq(z, -oo)), (0, Eq(z, -2)), (oo, Eq(z, 2)), (1, Eq(z, oo)), ((z**2/(z**2 - 4) - 3/(z**2 - 4))**z, True))

>>> limit((5**(1/x) + 3**(1/x))**x, x, z)
Piecewise((5, Eq(z, 0)), ((exp(log(3)/z) + exp(log(5)/z))**z, True))

>>> limit((sinh(x) + cosh(x) -1)/(4*x), x, z)    # this is the issue being solved above
Piecewise((1/4, Eq(z, 0)), (oo, Eq(z, oo)), ((exp(z) - 1)/(4*z), True))
>>> limit((sinh(x) + cosh(x) -1)/(4*x), x, z).subs(z, 0)
1/4

>>> limit(exp(1/x) , x, z)
Piecewise((oo, Eq(z, 0)), (exp(1/z), True))

>>> limit(1/sqrt(x), x, z, dir='-')
Piecewise((-oo*I, Eq(z, 0)), (1/sqrt(z), True))
```

I realized that explicit checks at `-oo` and `oo` are quite important because
1) They won't be coming under singularities usually 
2) Secondly this would lead to wrong answers . For eg if we don't have a check for them
```
>>> limit((1 + x)/x, x, z)
Piecewise((oo, Eq(z, 0)), ((z + 1)/z, True))
>>> limit((1 + x)/x, x, z).subs(z, oo)
nan
```

#### Other comments

The implementation currently works only for expressions have finite discontinuities but I feel this could be extended for expressions having periodic infinite discontinuities . Hence for something like an `imageset` for eg `limit(tan(x)/x, x, z)` or  `limit(tan(x), x, z)`  where we have a periodic repetition of discontinuous points , we could maybe try to calculate limit at the first point and generalize it overall !!
```
>>>singularities(tan(x)/x , x)
Union(FiniteSet(0), ImageSet(Lambda(_n, 2*_n*pi + pi/2), Integers), ImageSet(Lambda(_n, 2*_n*pi + 3*pi/2), Integers))
```
I wasn't sure how one could maybe implement this due to my inexperience with the ` Solvers` Module. Can we somehow get the generalized expression from the `ImageSet` ??  . Also I'll add tests as soon as the first set of review is done !

a contributor to the `series` module I have my fair share of idea of what sympy can achieve currently and what are it's limitations. Hence I make this issue  thinking what a user would expect out of the following expressions shown below 

Following basic pattern of growth of functions which is `const < log(x) < x**n < 2**x or exp(x) < factorial(x) < x**x` we have 
**On Master**

```
>>> O(2**x + factorial(x), (x, oo))
O(exp(x*log(2)) + factorial(x), (x, oo))

>>> O(2**x + factorial(x) + x**x, (x, oo))
O(exp(x*log(x)) + factorial(x), (x, oo))

>>> O(x + factorial(x), (x, oo))
O(x*(1 + factorial(x)/x), (x, oo))

```

**Expected Results:** I also ended up checking the results on other CAS and If i remember the results worked properly on `diofant` 
```
>>> O(2**x + factorial(x), (x, oo)) 
O(factorial(x), (x, oo))

>>> O(2**x + factorial(x) + x**x, (x, oo))
O((1/x)**(-x), (x, oo))

>>> O(x + factorial(x), (x, oo))
O( factorial(x) , (x, oo))

```

If you see the issues raised most issues a related to getting limits for simple piecewise functions working and I think that should be the focus. During my GSoC year (2022) ... I remember we couldn't get the limits for piecewise working because, there were so many ways to represent the exact same piecewise function 
```
    p0 = Piecewise((0, Or(x < -2, x > 2)), (1, True))
    p1 = Piecewise((0, x < -2), (0, x > 2), (1, True))
    p2 = Piecewise((0, x > 2), (0, x < -2), (1, True))
    p3 = Piecewise((0, x < -2), (1, x < 2), (0, True))
    p4 = Piecewise((0, x > 2), (1, x > -2), (0, True))
    p5 = Piecewise((1, And(-2< x, x < 2)), (0, True))
   
```
And we couldn't figure out a way to find limits let's say at 0 that would satisfy all these functions. The more cases we tried addressing the more unnecessary long and buggy the code became, hence my thought here would be to get simple equivalent piecewise functions (like the 6 above) to work together. 
limit at any point `x0` for all equivalent piecewise functions should result into the same output.
